titles: もしも今夜、月が消えたら？最初に壊れるもの
月が消えた地球：いちばん怖いのは「いちばん遅い変化」
月がなくなっても、地球は最初は気づかない
月のない世界：暗い夜、小さな潮、さまよう地軸
月が消えた0秒から1億年後まで、何が起きるのか
unique_angle: Most takes on this question list disasters as if they all hit at once. This one is told as a clock — second zero, first night, first tide, first year, then millions of years — and keeps an honest scorecard of measured facts, physics inferences and open scientific debate. The twist is that the orbit, the day and the oceans survive the first shock; the real threat is the slowest one, Earth's tilt, and even the experts disagree on how bad it would get (Laskar 1993 vs. Lissauer et al. 2011). The ending reframes the Moon as a lamp, a tide clock and a hand on the steering wheel of our seasons.
overview_ja: ある夜、月が音もなく消えたら何が起きるのかを、時間軸（0秒→初めての夜→最初の潮→1年後→数百万年後）に沿って描く。映画的な「地球が軌道から外れる」「巨大津波」といった誤解をまず科学的に否定し、本当に起きる変化（夜の暗さ、潮の縮小、生物のリズムの乱れ、日食の消滅）を示す。最大の山場は、最も遅く進む変化である地軸の傾きの不安定化で、Laskar（1993）とLissauerら（2011）の見解の違いも正直に紹介する。事実・推論・演出を区別し、仮説の限界を明示して終える。
why_interesting: Everyone has looked at the Moon; the premise needs no explanation.
It overturns the expected disaster-movie answer in the first minute, which rewards staying.
The time-ladder structure creates natural cliffhangers between chapters.
A real scientific disagreement (how chaotic Earth's tilt would become) gives the ending substance.
Visually rich: night skies, reefs, coastlines, eclipses, Earth from orbit.
hook: 今夜、午後9時41分。月が、消えました。爆発も、閃光もありません。では、最初に壊れるのは何でしょうか。いちばん危険な変化は、いちばんゆっくりやって来るのです。

claims_to_verify: Location of the Earth–Moon barycenter (inside Earth, ~4,700 km from the center)
Earth's mean orbital speed around the Sun
Illuminance of a full Moon vs a moonless clear sky
Dung beetles navigating by polarized moonlight and the Milky Way
Coral spawning linked to moonlight (cry2 gene)
Sun's tidal force relative to the Moon's
Spring and neap tides come from Sun–Moon alignment
Moon recession rate from lunar laser ranging (3.8 cm/yr)
Tidal braking lengthens the day by ~2 ms per century
Laskar et al. 1993: moonless obliquity chaotic 0°–85°
Lissauer et al. 2011: moonless obliquity variations much narrower
